**Supported Facts**

The current official MCP revision is `2026-07-28`, and in that revision the protocol is stateless: the modern protocol removed the `initialize` / `notifications/initialized` handshake. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning)

For a modern stdio server, version selection is not done by a session handshake. Each request carries its protocol version in `_meta.io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion`, and if the server does not support that version it must return `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError` with the versions it does support. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic)

A modern server must also treat `_meta.io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities` as required on every request, and must reject a request missing required `_meta` fields with JSON-RPC `-32602` (`Invalid params`). (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic)

Servers must not rely on undeclared client capabilities; if a request needs a capability the client did not declare, the server must return `MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError` (`-32021`). (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic)

Servers must implement `server/discover`, and clients may use it before any other request to learn supported versions, capabilities, and identity. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/discover)

On stdio, the server reads JSON-RPC from `stdin` and writes JSON-RPC to `stdout`; each message is exactly one JSON-RPC request, notification, or response; messages are newline-delimited and must not contain embedded newlines. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/stdio)

On stdio, the server may write UTF-8 log text to `stderr`

**Supported Facts**

The current official MCP revision is `2026-07-28`, and in that revision the protocol is stateless: the modern protocol removed the `initialize` / `notifications/initialized` handshake. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning)

For a modern stdio server, version selection is not done by a session handshake. Each request carries its protocol version in `_meta.io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion`, and if the server does not support that version it must return `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError` with the versions it does support. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic)

A modern server must also treat `_meta.io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities` as required on every request, and must reject a request missing required `_meta` fields with JSON-RPC `-32602` (`Invalid params`). (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic)

Servers must not rely on undeclared client capabilities; if a request needs a capability the client did not declare, the server must return `MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError` (`-32021`). (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic)

Servers must implement `server/discover`, and clients may use it before any other request to learn supported versions, capabilities, and identity. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/discover)

On stdio, the server reads JSON-RPC from `stdin` and writes JSON-RPC to `stdout`; each message is exactly one JSON-RPC request, notification, or response; messages are newline-delimited and must not contain embedded newlines. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/stdio)

On stdio, the server may write UTF-8 log text to `stderr`, but it must not write anything to `stdout` that is not a valid MCP message. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/stdio)

On stdio, there is no header layer; request metadata stays in the JSON-RPC body under `_meta`. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/stdio)

On stdio, the server must not initiate JSON-RPC requests on `stdout`; server output is limited to responses and notifications. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/stdio)

If a server supports tools, it must declare the `tools` capability. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools)

A server that declares `tools` must answer `tools/list` with the tools currently available to the requesting client. That set may be empty, may change over time, and may vary by per-request authorization, but it must not vary by connection or as a side effect of other requests on the connection. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools)

The spec says the server should return tools in a deterministic order. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools)

`tools/list` is a paginated request: the request params are `PaginatedRequestParams`, which means `_meta` is required and `cursor` is optional. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/schema)

A successful `tools/list` response is `ListToolsResultResponse`, whose `result` is `ListToolsResult`. In the current protocol version, `ListToolsResult` includes `resultType`, `ttlMs`, `cacheScope`, and `tools`, with `nextCursor` optional. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/schema)

For this protocol version, the server must include `resultType` in the result. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/schema)

Each tool definition includes `name`, optional `title`, `description`, optional `icons`, and `inputSchema`; `inputSchema` must be a valid JSON Schema object, not `null`. `outputSchema` and `annotations` are optional. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools)

If the server advertised `tools.listChanged`, then when the tool list changes it should send `notifications/tools/list_changed` to clients that opened a `subscriptions/listen` stream with `toolsListChanged: true`. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools)

**Legacy `initialize`**

The current official spec classifies `initialize` as legacy behavior: legacy versions are `2025-11-25` and earlier, while modern versions are `2026-07-28` and later. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning)

A server that wants to support both modern and legacy clients may implement both behaviors. On stdio, a dual-era client should probe with `server/discover` first; if it gets a recognized modern error such as `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError`, it stays in the modern flow, and if it gets some other error or no timely response, it falls back to legacy `initialize`. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/stdio)

The current spec also says a modern-only server should name the protocol versions it supports in any error it returns to an `initialize` request, because legacy clients have no forward-upgrade mechanism. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning)

In the official legacy lifecycle spec (`2025-11-25`), initialization had to be the first interaction; the client sent `initialize` with protocol version, client capabilities, and client info; the server responded with its protocol version, server capabilities, and server info; then the client sent `notifications/initialized`. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/lifecycle)

That same legacy page says the client should not send non-ping requests before the `initialize` response, and the server should not send non-ping, non-logging requests before `notifications/initialized`. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/lifecycle)

The legacy page also says version negotiation during `initialize` worked by the client sending a supported version, the server echoing it if supported or returning another supported version if not, and the client disconnecting if it could not support the server’s chosen version. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/lifecycle)

**Inference**

Therefore, for a stdio server that implements only the current modern MCP revision, there is no required `initialize` exchange at all; the required behavior is per-request `_meta` handling, version rejection via `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError` when needed, `server/discover`, and newline-delimited JSON-RPC framing over stdio. This conclusion is an inference from the current spec’s removal of `initialize`, its per-request versioning rules, and its stdio transport rules. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/stdio)

**Disagreement / Uncertainty / Lack Of Good Evidence**

The main point of potential confusion is that the question assumes `initialize` is part of the current stdio flow, but the current official revision treats it as legacy compatibility, not as part of the modern protocol. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog)

I do not have direct official evidence for a modern `initialize` request or response shape, because the current `2026-07-28` spec removed that handshake; the only official evidence I found for `initialize` semantics is in the backward-compatibility rules and the older legacy lifecycle page. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/lifecycle)

# Tools

# Specification

<div id="enable-section-numbers" />

[Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) (MCP) is an open protocol that
enables seamless integration between LLM applications and external data sources and
tools. Whether you're building an AI-powered IDE, enhancing a chat interface, or creating
custom AI workflows, MCP provides a standardized way to connect LLMs with the context
they need.

This specification defines the authoritative protocol requirements, based on the
TypeScript schema in
[schema.ts](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/specification/blob/main/schema/2026-07-28/schema.ts).

For implementation guides and examples, visit
[modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io).

\[[RFC8174](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8174)] when, and only when, they
appear in all capitals, as shown here.

* **Hosts**: LLM applications that initiate connections
* **Clients**: Connectors within the host application
* **Servers**: Services that provide context and capabilities

# Versioning and Compatibility

<div id="enable-section-numbers" />

This page defines how a client and server agree on what they are speaking:
the protocol version, declared on every request; optional extensions,
negotiated through capabilities; and interoperability with earlier,
handshake-based protocol revisions.

There is no negotiation handshake. Every request carries its protocol
version, and the server accepts or rejects each request independently:

```mermaid theme={null}
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Server

    Client->>Server: request (with `_meta`)
    alt server supports requested version
        Server-->>Client: result
    else version unsupported
        Server-->>Client: UnsupportedProtocolVersionError
        Note over Client,Server: Client retries with a mutually supported version
    end
```

## Terminology

This page uses the following terms for interoperability across protocol
revisions:

* **Modern**: protocol versions that convey version, identity, and
  capabilities as per-request metadata (revision `2026-07-28` and later).
* **Legacy**: protocol versions that establish a session with an
  `initialize` handshake (`2025-11-25` and earlier).
* **Dual-era**: an implementation that supports both modern and legacy
  versions.

[`_meta`](/specification/2026-07-28/basic/index#meta) field. On HTTP, this is
also carried in the
[`MCP-Protocol-Version` header](/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/streamable-http#protocol-version-header).

If the server does not implement the requested version (whether the version
is unknown to the server, or is a known version the server has chosen not to

# Overview

<div id="enable-section-numbers" />

This page defines what a transport must provide to carry MCP messages, the
standard transport bindings, and the requirements for defining new ones.

Protocol semantics are identical on every transport. A transport is a
**binding**: it defines how messages are framed and delivered, how request
metadata is carried, and how cancellation and termination are signaled. It
does not define what the messages mean: the
[message patterns](/specification/2026-07-28/basic/patterns) are part of the core
protocol and are the same on every binding. The binding pages specify the
standard transports:

1. [stdio](/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/stdio): newline-delimited
   messages over the standard streams of a client-launched subprocess.
2. [Streamable HTTP](/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/streamable-http):
   each message is an HTTP POST to a single MCP endpoint; replies arrive as
   a JSON object or a request-scoped SSE stream.

It is also possible for clients and servers to implement
[custom transports](#custom-transports).

## Messages

MCP uses JSON-RPC to encode messages. JSON-RPC messages **MUST** be UTF-8
encoded.

A binding **MUST** deliver client-sent *requests* and *notifications* to the
server, and server-sent *responses* and *notifications* to the client. No
other message direction exists: per the
[message patterns](/specification/2026-07-28/basic/patterns), servers do not
initiate JSON-RPC requests and clients do not send JSON-RPC responses.

## Request Metadata

All protocol metadata travels in the message body: every request carries its
protocol version and client capabilities in
[`_meta.io.modelcontextprotocol/*`](/specification/2026-07-28/basic/index#meta)
fields.

# Tools

<div id="enable-section-numbers" />

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) allows servers to expose tools that can be invoked by
language models. Tools enable models to interact with external systems, such as querying
databases, calling APIs, or performing computations. Each tool is uniquely identified by
a name and includes metadata describing its schema.

<Note>
  For brevity, the request examples on this page omit the `_meta` request
  metadata (`io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion`,
  `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo`, and
  `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities`). Every request **MUST** include
  the required `_meta` fields; see
  [`_meta`](/specification/2026-07-28/basic/index#meta).
</Note>

## User Interaction Model

Tools in MCP are designed to be **model-controlled**, meaning that the language model can
discover and invoke tools automatically based on its contextual understanding and the
user's prompts.

However, implementations are free to expose tools through any interface pattern that
suits their needs—the protocol itself does not mandate any specific user
interaction model.

<Warning>
  For trust & safety and security, there **SHOULD** always
  be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations.

  Applications **SHOULD**:

  * Provide UI that makes clear which tools are being exposed to the AI model
  * Insert clear visual indicators when tools are invoked
  * Present confirmation prompts to the user for operations, to ensure a human is in the
    loop
</Warning>

Servers that support tools **MUST** declare the `tools` capability:

```json theme={null}
{
  "capabilities": {
    "tools": {
      "listChanged": true
    }
  }
}
```

# stdio

<div id="enable-section-numbers" />

In the **stdio** transport, the client launches the MCP server as a subprocess.
The two ends communicate over the subprocess's standard streams:

* The server reads JSON-RPC messages from `stdin` and writes JSON-RPC messages to
  `stdout`.
* Each message is a single JSON-RPC request, notification, or response.
* Messages are delimited by newlines, and **MUST NOT** contain embedded newlines.
* The server **MAY** write UTF-8 strings to `stderr` for any logging purposes
  including informational, debug, and error messages.
* The client **MAY** capture, forward, or ignore the server's `stderr` output and
  **SHOULD NOT** assume `stderr` output indicates error conditions.
* The server **MUST NOT** write anything to its `stdout` that is not a valid MCP
  message.
* The client **MUST NOT** write anything to the server's `stdin` that is not a
  valid MCP message.

Standard streams are the canonical channel, but nothing in this binding
depends on them except the process lifecycle. The wire format (one
newline-delimited JSON-RPC message per line over a reliable bidirectional
byte stream) works unchanged over Unix domain sockets, TCP connections, or
any similar channel.
[Custom transports](/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports#custom-transports)
built on such streams **SHOULD** reuse this framing and the message rules on
this page; only the subprocess-specific aspects (launch, `stderr`, shutdown
by closing the stream, process restart) need channel-specific equivalents.

## Sending Messages

The client sends messages by writing JSON-RPC *requests* and *notifications*
to the server's `stdin`, one message per line. The client **MUST NOT** write
JSON-RPC *responses*.

# Overview

<div id="enable-section-numbers" />

The Model Context Protocol consists of several key components that work together:

* **Base Protocol**: Core JSON-RPC message types
* **Versioning and Compatibility**: Protocol version negotiation, extension negotiation, and interoperability with earlier protocol revisions
* **Message Patterns**: Messaging patterns supported by the core protocol including request and response, multi round-trip requests (MRTR), and subscribe and notify
* **Authorization**: Authentication and authorization framework for HTTP-based transports
* **Server Features**: Resources, prompts, and tools exposed by servers
* **Client Features**: Elicitation, sampling and root directory lists provided by clients
* **Utilities**: Cross-cutting concerns like logging and argument completion

All implementations **MUST** support the base protocol, versioning,
and the message patterns. Other components **MAY** be implemented based on the specific needs of the
application.

These protocol layers establish clear separation of concerns while enabling rich
interactions between clients and servers. The modular design allows implementations to
support exactly the features they need.

# Transports

<div id="enable-section-numbers" />

MCP uses JSON-RPC to encode messages. JSON-RPC messages **MUST** be UTF-8 encoded.

The protocol currently defines two standard transport mechanisms for client-server
communication:

1. [stdio](#stdio), communication over standard in and standard out
2. [Streamable HTTP](#streamable-http)

Clients **SHOULD** support stdio whenever possible.

It is also possible for clients and servers to implement
[custom transports](#custom-transports) in a pluggable fashion.

## stdio

In the **stdio** transport:

* The client launches the MCP server as a subprocess.
* The server reads JSON-RPC messages from its standard input (`stdin`) and sends messages
  to its standard output (`stdout`).
* Messages are individual JSON-RPC requests, notifications, or responses.
* Messages are delimited by newlines, and **MUST NOT** contain embedded newlines.
* The server **MAY** write UTF-8 strings to its standard error (`stderr`) for any
  logging purposes including informational, debug, and error messages.
* The client **MAY** capture, forward, or ignore the server's `stderr` output
  and **SHOULD NOT** assume `stderr` output indicates error conditions.
* The server **MUST NOT** write anything to its `stdout` that is not a valid MCP message.
* The client **MUST NOT** write anything to the server's `stdin` that is not a valid MCP
  message.

# Pagination

<div id="enable-section-numbers" />

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) supports paginating list operations that may return
large result sets. Pagination allows servers to yield results in smaller chunks rather
than all at once.

Pagination is especially important when connecting to external services over the
internet, but also useful for local integrations to avoid performance issues with large
data sets.

<Note>

  the required `_meta` fields; see
  [`_meta`](/specification/2026-07-28/basic/index#meta).
</Note>

## Pagination Model

Pagination in MCP uses an opaque cursor-based approach, instead of numbered pages.

* The **cursor** is an opaque string token, representing a position in the result set
* **Page size** is determined by the server, and clients **MUST NOT** assume a fixed page
  size

## Response Format

Pagination starts when the server sends a **response** that includes:

* The current page of results
* An optional `nextCursor` field if more results exist

```json theme={null}
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": "123",
  "result": {
    "resultType": "complete",
    "resources": [...],
    "nextCursor": "eyJwYWdlIjogM30=",
    "ttlMs": 300000,
    "cacheScope": "public"
  }
}
```

## Request Format

After receiving a cursor, the client can *continue* paginating by issuing a request
including that cursor:

```json theme={null}
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": "124",
  "method": "resources/list",
  "params": {
    "cursor": "eyJwYWdlIjogMn0="
  }
}
```

## Short answer up front

The premise of the question needs one correction before anything else: **the current official MCP specification revision, `2026-07-28`, no longer has an `initialize` handshake at all.** The spec's versioning page states plainly: "The **current** protocol version is [**2026-07-28**]" and that revisions are marked Draft / Current / Final ([versioning](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/versioning)). The spec index links all its sections at `/specification/2026-07-28/...` and cites `schema/2026-07-28/schema.ts` as authoritative ([specification index](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/)).

In that revision, `initialize` is classified as **"legacy"** — the spec's own term for "protocol versions that establish a session with an `initialize` handshake (`2025-11-25` and earlier)", versus **"modern"** versions that "convey version, identity, and capabilities as per-request metadata (revision `2026-07-28` and later)" ([versioning & compatibility](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning)).

So I'll answer twice: what the current spec requires, and what the legacy `initialize` handshake required (still relevant for interop).

---

## 1. Current spec (2026-07-28): what a stdio server MUST do

### Message framing — essentially unchanged

From the [stdio binding](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/stdio):

- Server reads JSON-RPC from `stdin`, writes JSON-RPC to `stdout`.
- "Each message is a single JSON-RPC request, notification, or response."
- "Messages are delimited by newlines, and **MUST NOT** contain embedded newlines."
- Server **MAY** write UTF-8 strings to `stderr` for logging; the client **MAY** capture/forward/ignore it and **SHOULD NOT** assume `stderr` output indicates errors.
- Server **MUST NOT** write anything to `stdout` that is not a valid MCP message; client **MUST NOT** write anything to `stdin` that isn't one.
- JSON-RPC messages **MUST** be UTF-8 encoded ([transports overview](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports)).

Direction rules are now tighter than most people remember: "The server **MUST NOT** write JSON-RPC *requests* to `stdout`," and the client **MUST NOT** write JSON-RPC *responses*. Server→client interaction happens via `InputRequiredResult` replies instead ([stdio](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/stdio)). Notifications delivered on a `subscriptions/listen` stream **MUST** carry `io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId` in `_meta` so the client can correlate them.

There is no `Content-Length` header framing anywhere in MCP stdio — it is line-delimited JSON, unlike LSP.

### Version negotiation — no handshake, per-request

> "There is no negotiation handshake. Every request carries its protocol version, and the server accepts or rejects each request independently." ([versioning & compatibility](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning))

Concretely, for a stdio server:

- Every client request carries `_meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion"]` (**required**) and `_meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities"]` (**required**); `clientInfo` is optional but clients **SHOULD** send it ([`_meta`](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/index)).
- "A request missing any required field is malformed; the server **MUST** reject it with JSON-RPC error code `-32602` (Invalid params)."
- If the server doesn't implement the requested version it **MUST** return `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError`, code **`-32022`**, with `data.supported` listing versions it does support and `data.requested`. The client **SHOULD** then retry with a mutually supported version.
- "A server **MUST NOT** rely on capabilities the client has not declared" — if it needs an undeclared capability it **MUST** return `MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError` (`-32021`) with `data.requiredCapabilities`.
- Servers **SHOULD** include `_meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo"]` in every result.
- On stdio there is no header layer; all metadata is inline in the body ([stdio](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/stdio)). The `MCP-Protocol-Version` header is Streamable-HTTP-only.

### `server/discover` is mandatory

"Servers **MUST** implement `server/discover`" ([discovery](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/discover); repeated in [versioning](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning)). It returns `supportedVersions`, `capabilities`, optional `instructions`, and `serverInfo` in `_meta`. Calling it is optional *for clients*; implementing it is not optional for servers.

### Statelessness

This is the big behavioral requirement people miss when porting: "Servers **MUST NOT** rely on prior requests over the same connection to establish context (e.g., capabilities, protocol version, client identity)." A stdio process is explicitly **not** a session — "clients may interleave unrelated requests on the same transport, and a server must not treat connection or process identity as a proxy for conversation or session continuity" ([base protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/index)).

### `tools/list`

From [server/tools](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools):

- Servers supporting tools **MUST** declare the `tools` capability (with optional `listChanged`).
- They **MUST** respond to `tools/list` with the currently available set. It **MAY** be empty and **MAY** change over time, but **MUST NOT** vary per-connection or as a side effect of other requests. It **MAY** vary by the authorization presented on the request.
- Servers **SHOULD** return tools in deterministic order.
- The result **MUST** include `resultType` (`"complete"`), per the general rule that "The `result` **MUST** include a `resultType` field" ([base protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/index)). Clients **MUST** treat an absent `resultType` as `"complete"` for backward compatibility.
- `inputSchema` **MUST** be a valid JSON Schema object (not `null`), defaulting to JSON Schema 2020-12 absent `$schema`. If `outputSchema` is given, servers **MUST** produce conforming structured results.
- Pagination: cursors are opaque; "Page size is determined by the server, and clients **MUST NOT** assume a fixed page size"; clients **SHOULD** treat missing `nextCursor` as end of results; an empty string is a valid cursor and **MUST NOT** be treated as the end; invalid cursors **SHOULD** yield `-32602` ([pagination](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/utilities/pagination)).
- `notifications/tools/list_changed` is now tied to `subscriptions/listen` with `toolsListChanged: true`, not broadcast freely.

### Shutdown

Client **SHOULD** close stdin, wait, then forcibly terminate. Notably: "Servers **SHOULD** exit promptly when their standard input is closed or reads return end-of-file. This is the primary graceful-shutdown signal and the only portable one" ([stdio](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/stdio)).

## 2. Legacy (2025-11-25 and earlier): the `initialize` handshake

If your question is really "what does my existing stdio server need to do," this is likely the relevant text ([2025-11-25 lifecycle](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/lifecycle)):

- The initialization phase **MUST** be the first interaction. Client **MUST** send `initialize` with `protocolVersion`, `capabilities`, `clientInfo`.
- The server **MUST** respond with its own capabilities and information (`protocolVersion`, `capabilities`, `serverInfo`, optional `instructions`).
- The client **MUST** then send `notifications/initialized`.
- Version negotiation: client **MUST** send a version it supports, **SHOULD** be the latest. "If the server supports the requested protocol version, it **MUST** respond with the same version. Otherwise, the server **MUST** respond with another protocol version it supports," **SHOULD** be the server's latest. If the client doesn't support the server's answer, it **SHOULD** disconnect.
- Client **SHOULD NOT** send requests other than pings before the `initialize` response; server **SHOULD NOT** send requests other than pings and logging before `initialized`.
- Both parties **MUST** respect the negotiated version and **MUST** only use negotiated capabilities.

Framing in 2025-11-25 stdio is textually identical to the current text (newline-delimited, no embedded newlines, UTF-8, nothing non-MCP on stdout) ([2025-11-25 transports](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/transports)).

---

## 3. Interop between the two eras

The spec gives explicit stdio mechanics ([stdio backward compatibility](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/stdio), [compatibility matrix](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning)):

- A dual-era client **SHOULD** probe with `server/discover` first. `DiscoverResult` ⇒ modern. A recognized modern error like `-32022` ⇒ modern, retry with a supported version, do **not** fall back. Any other error, or a timeout ⇒ legacy, fall back to `initialize`.
- "The fallback **MUST NOT** be keyed to one specific error code" — legacy servers reply to unknown pre-`initialize` methods with implementation-defined errors (commonly `-32601` or `-32602`) or not at all.
- Modern client + legacy server = **fails**; legacy client + modern server = **fails** (legacy clients have no fall-forward). A modern-only server **SHOULD** name its supported versions in whatever error it returns to `initialize`, since that error may be the only diagnostic a legacy client can show.
- A dual-era server picks its era from how the client opens, and **MAY** serve both concurrently on the same process.

## Epistemic status

**Directly supported by the cited spec pages:** everything above with a quoted MUST/SHOULD.

**Inference, not stated in the spec:** that the `2026-07-28` per-request model is a substantial rewrite likely to outrun SDK support — the removal of `initialize`, mandatory `server/discover`, `resultType`, and enforced statelessness are large enough changes that a server built against 2025-11-25 will not satisfy 2026-07-28 without work. That's my reading of the diff, not a spec claim.

**Not verified — I did not check this:** whether the official TypeScript/Python SDKs currently implement `2026-07-28`, and what real-world clients (Claude Desktop, IDEs) negotiate today. Search results surfaced a [release-candidate blog post](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28-release-candidate/) and one search snippet asserted 2025-11-25 was still current with 2026-07-28 as an RC — that snippet is contradicted by the spec site itself, which now marks 2026-07-28 as Current, and I'm going with the spec site. If you need SDK-level ground truth, the schema files under `schema/2026-07-28/` in the [specification repo](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/specification) are the authoritative check.

**A genuine ambiguity in the docs:** `/specification/2026-07-28/basic/lifecycle` serves the "Versioning and Compatibility" page rather than a lifecycle page — the lifecycle concept was folded into versioning. I mention it because a stale bookmark to that URL now returns materially different content than it used to.
